**Yes, the cable can cap your charging speed.** The charger and device negotiate power, but a cable can only carry what it's rated for. Cables rated for more than 3A (60W) carry an e-marker chip that tells the charger what the cable can safely handle.

**What the ratings mean**
- **60W (20V, 3A):** Most basic USB-C cables. Fine for phones, tablets, and smaller laptops.
- **100W (20V, 5A):** Needs an e-marker. USB-IF says 100W USB-C to USB-C cables were replaced by 240W cables in the spec, and it stopped certifying new 100W cables on December 22, 2021 ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations), [USB-IF compliance updates](https://compliance.usb.org/index.asp?Format=Standard&UpdateFile=Cables+and+Connectors&pubDate=20261005)). 100W cables are still sold, but they aren't a certified category now.
- **240W (48V, 5A, EPR):** Needs an e-marker and the 240W logo. USB PD 3.1 adds 28V, 36V, and 48V levels for up to 140W, 180W, and 240W ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)).

USB-IF says certified USB-C to USB-C cables must carry either a 60W or 240W logo ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)). The logo is the easiest way to check what a cable supports.

**How to pick**
- **Phone, tablet, or earbuds:** A 60W cable is plenty.
- **Laptop at 65-100W:** Use a 5A/e-marked cable (100W or 240W), since a 60W cable would hold you to about 60W.
- **Laptop or dock above 100W:** You need a 240W-rated cable.
- A cable can't add power beyond what the charger and device support. Your device and charger still set the ceiling, and the cable only sets a cap on top of that.
- Also keep in mind that power rating and data speed are separate. A 240W cable can still be USB 2.0-only for data.

**One option I found:** the [Baseus USB-C to USB-C Cable, 100W](https://dealectric.com/go/baseus-usb-c-cable-100w) is rated 100W (5A, e-marked) and starts at $9.99 for 1 m ($12.99 for 2 m, $16.99 for 3 m). It suits laptops up to 100W, but it's USB 2.0 data only (480 Mbps), has no video output, and isn't rated for 140W or 240W. Baseus also notes it doesn't support charging iPad Pro. The listing doesn't say whether it's USB-IF certified, so I can't confirm that. (This is an affiliate link; Dealectric is paid if you buy, at no cost to you.)

I only found details for that one cable, so I can't compare specific 60W or 240W products. If you tell me your device and charger wattage, I can narrow down what you need.
